dossier.summary: The project provides a substantial controlled simulation of regression-based GATE estimation, with analytical bias predictions, multiple graph families and mechanisms, and delivered replicate-level results. Its evidence supports persistent misspecification bias, a substantial variance cost, and design-dependent benefits of clustering within the studied settings. The abstract overstates bias dominance and the failure of richer estimators, while the implemented lasso comparison and auxiliary coverage calculations differ from their descriptions. Reproduction is partly supported by fixed seeds and compact results, but missing build inputs, incorrect default paths, and raw-only analysis scripts prevent the advertised workflow from running as delivered. The recorded commands support substantial experimental provenance, although empty tool-result bodies limit conclusions about every reported quantity.

claims.quote: Under Bernoulli($p$) assignment and one-hop spillover, the population bias is $\gamma(s-1)$ for an exactly computable $s$; it matches 144 noiseless cells within Monte-Carlo error, does not shrink with $n$ ($+2.53\to+2.49$ from $n=10^3$ to $2\cdot10^4$), is proportional to the interference strength in 14 of 16 tested groups, and changes sign with $p$.
On Erd\H{o}s--R\'enyi graphs the standard deviation scales as $n^{-0.501\pm0.005}d^{0.495\pm0.006}$.

At the grid's $(n,d,\sigma)$ the estimator beats the difference in means once interference is moderate, but has 5.5--18.6 times its SD when there is none; the crossover strength scales as $n^{-0.49}d^{1.01}$ and the SD ratio as $d^{1.0}$.
Under nonlinear spillover bias dominates and richer fits (penalised OLS, tuned boosting) do not help; intervals that ignore dependence under-cover, and a cluster bootstrap does not reach 95\% either.
Heavy-tailed degrees raise neither SD nor bias in a matched test, and the Stanford3 case where graph clusters hurt replicates on a second seed.

\textbf{What the evidence says.} The regression-based GATE estimator is accurate when its exposure model is right and the interference is not weak, and its failure is mostly a \emph{bias} problem that more data do not cure:
scope_words: when its exposure model is right

claims.quote: The two causes respond to opposite remedies (a richer model removes bias and adds variance; more data remove variance only), so accuracy reports should give bias and SD separately and include a correctly specified control.
Standard errors that ignore dependence overstate precision, and no interval, including a cluster bootstrap, reaches nominal coverage on average once the bias is present.

issues.quote: Under nonlinear spillover bias dominates and richer fits (penalised OLS, tuned boosting) do not help;
issues.why: Section 4.5 reports bias exceeding half of MSE in only 33%, 38% and 67% of concave, convex and sigmoid cells respectively; bias is not dominant in most of the nonlinear cells combined. Table 9 also shows tuned boosting beating OLS in 83% of sigmoid cells at p=0.5, so the abstract's unqualified statement exceeds the reported evidence.

issues.quote: Simulations with exactly known truth (806 planned cells over four synthetic and two Facebook graphs, five outcome mechanisms, four designs, four simulated worlds per cell; 172 cells added after the first results) separate its bias from its variance.
issues.why: The abstract counts 172 added cells, but results.tex line 5 and Table 2 report 816 added cells and 1622 overall. The abstract omits the second-seed and later analysis grids.

issues.quote: it wins only where OLS$(z,f)$ is badly biased (concave at $p=0.1$: 0.51; sigmoid: 0.40--0.59).
issues.why: Table 9 and experiments.py lines 243–251 show tuned boosting was run only at p=0.5. The 0.51 concave p=0.1 and 0.59 sigmoid ratios belong to untuned boosting; attributing these to tuned boosting mixes the two comparisons.

issues.quote: \emph{while its neighbours stay untreated}, and is biased for the GATE by the spillover.
issues.why: Under Bernoulli assignment the difference in means averages over neighbors' random treatment assignments, rather than fixing all neighbors untreated. This distinction matters for nonlinear or interacting potential outcomes.

presentation.why: Figure 1 is reduced to 55% of the text width; the six small panels and legend require substantial magnification to read. Figures 3–6 on pages 6–8 also have very small ticks and legends.
Table 1's caption prints internal result paths and a generating script name. Similar file paths occupy appendix captions and prose, interrupting the scientific presentation.
Figure 10's caption promises bias and RMSE, but both plotted rows are RMSE, split by Bernoulli and Louvain designs. The caption does not describe the displayed panels.

paper_mismatches.why: Both two-hop sweeps use gamma=1.0 and gamma2=1.0, rather than the appendix's gamma2=0.5 and default gamma=2. The delivered results describe a different allocation of spillover strength.

paper_mismatches.paper_quote: Richer fits were unpenalised, ridge/lasso-penalised or boosted with a small tuning grid
paper_mismatches.why: Lasso coefficients are discarded after feature selection; the final estimate uses an unpenalized least-squares refit at lines 158–161. The reported failure does not establish the stated result for a lasso-penalized GATE fit.

paper_mismatches.paper_quote: the interval bias$\pm1.96\,$SE with the aggregation rule (larger of replicate- and world-level SE) covers the reference in $0.968$ of draws
paper_mismatches.why: The comparison uses disjoint remaining worlds and multiplies SE by sqrt(1+W/(20-W)); at W=4 the tested interval is about 11.8% wider than stated. Table 11 labels the target as the 20-world mean, whereas the code uses the remaining-world mean.

paper_mismatches.paper_quote: the closed form for finite and heterogeneous degrees
paper_mismatches.why: The formula uses a representative synthetic graph with seed=0, not the actual degree sequences of the simulation worlds (runner.py line 45 uses seed*1000+w). This qualifies the claim that agreement checks use the actual degree mixture; the real graphs are fixed.

evaluation_errors.why: Coverage labelled as covering E[tau-hat] uses the mean of the same replicates within each world as its target (lines 32 and 39). Self-inclusion shrinks estimation deviations and the target is conditional on the world, so these reported expectation-coverage values do not estimate the stated unconditional quantity; the main GATE-coverage comparisons are unaffected.

problems.why: main.tex requires iclr2027_conference and math_commands.tex, neither delivered; Makefile points to ../venue/iclr2027 and ../figures/out, which are absent at those relative locations in this layout. MANIFEST.json reports no omitted files.

results/figures/scripts/common.py lines 13–15 resolve the input directory to /in/results/results/summary, using a layout intended for a top-level figures folder. FIGTAB_RESULTS must be overridden to use the delivered summaries.

coverage_analysis.py lines 59–62 and world_uncertainty.py lines 24–32 read only results/raw, which is absent. The delivered compact data can support these calculations but the scripts do not implement a compact-data fallback, contrary to the claim that every table can be regenerated without raw files.

The installation command in /in/REPRODUCE.md line 8 installs code/requirements.lock, which does not include matplotlib. Figure scripts import matplotlib, so that stated dependency installation is insufficient to regenerate the figures.

process_notes: Experiments counts program_runs entries, including failed attempts, sharded jobs, pilots and result-producing analyses; it is not the number of grid cells or independent worlds.
failed_then_fixed follows the recovered field of failures in tables.json.

Rework counts two confirmed numerical-regeneration episodes after first paper use: post_freeze.py reruns t14/t15 while adding the completed second-seed analysis (root/experiment-repo/a2d5cd0758d830f218820c7142f3117a#toolu_01LEzyRuHgLHr3GFRZKQmKHo), and the bulk reaggregation of e1–e12 summaries (root/experiment-repo/a2d5cd0758d830f218820c7142f3117a#toolu_01DbqgBeJVYVi1JQNm56w5Xq). New exploratory grids and figure-formatting rebuilds are excluded; empty outputs prevent a complete per-file rewrite history.

All examined trajectory observation content fields are empty. fields.json confirms commands and timings are recorded but exit codes are unavailable; no missing-work finding is inferred from this limitation.

integrity.why: The examined comparisons report synthetic grid conditions and estimator families rather than selecting a hidden winning test configuration. Boosting is selected by outcome-prediction cross-validation on the first assignment in each world; the paper states this protocol. Outcome truth is used to compare estimators, not to tune the reported GATE estimator. Command result bodies are empty, so this finding is limited to the recorded commands and delivered code.

The record shows aggregation fixes, added bootstrap diagnostics, revised world-subset comparisons, and post-result hypothesis rules. The paper discloses exploratory additions and post-result thresholds. The temporary standard-error multipliers were a test-sensitivity check followed by restoration. The world-interval description and changed verdict rule are recorded separately as paper/code discrepancies; the available record does not establish an undisclosed favorable change behind the main evaluation.

Outcomes and exact GATEs are generated by the simulation. Reading their truth for evaluation and constructing the explicitly labelled oracle controls is part of the stated design; no held-out outcome labels forbidden to the ordinary estimator were identified. Cross-validation uses the assignment's observed outcomes, as described.

The delivered numerical files have corresponding generation commands and simulation jobs. However, trajectory observations contain empty result bodies and fields.json states that exit codes are unavailable; several commands are truncated. This supports file-level provenance but cannot establish that every textual quantity, including the compact-summary discrepancy, was actually emitted by a recorded run.
